name: POPE (Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation)
description: POPE is a polling-based object probing evaluation dataset for evaluating object hallucination in large vision-language models (LVLMs). It converts hallucination evaluation into a binary classification task by prompting LVLMs with simple Yes-or-No questions about objects in images (e.g., 'Is there a car in the image?'). The dataset is built on MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA, using three sampling strategies (Random, Popular, Adversarial) to probe whether LVLMs hallucinate frequently appearing or co-occurring objects.
creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
citeAs: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen. Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset is constructed from existing image datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA). For MSCOCO, 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects are randomly selected from the validation set. Ground-truth objects are obtained either from human annotations or from automatic segmentation using SEEM. Negative (non-existent) objects are sampled using three strategies: Random, Popular, and Adversarial sampling. Each image is associated with 6 polling questions (l=6), with a 1:1 ratio of ground-truth to non-existent objects.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images and object annotations from MSCOCO validation set (Lin et al., 2014), A-OKVQA (Schwenk et al., 2022), and GQA (Hudson and Manning, 2019). For MSCOCO CHAIR evaluation, 2,000 images with annotations about contained objects and human-labeled captions are randomly sampled from the validation set.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Three negative object sampling strategies are applied: (1) Random Sampling: randomly sample objects not present in the image; (2) Popular Sampling: select the top-k most frequent objects in the whole dataset that do not exist in the current image, where k = l/2; (3) Adversarial Sampling: rank all objects by co-occurrence frequency with ground-truth objects and select top-k frequent ones not present in the image. Ground-truth and non-existent objects are set at a 1:1 ratio for label balance.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For MSCOCO, 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects in annotations are randomly selected. For CHAIR evaluation, 2,000 images are sampled from the MSCOCO validation set, considering only 80 objects appearing in the MSCOCO segmentation challenge. For unannotated datasets (A-OKVQA, GQA), SEEM automatic segmentation tool is used to annotate images and extract objects. Questions are formulated using the template 'Is there a/an <object> in the image?'
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Ground-truth object labels are derived from existing human annotations in MSCOCO. For datasets without annotations (A-OKVQA, GQA), the automatic segmentation tool SEEM (Zou et al., 2023) is used to generate object annotations. Polling questions are constructed by pairing ground-truth objects (answer: 'Yes') and sampled non-existent objects (answer: 'No') with a question template.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) automatic segmentation tool for unannotated datasets; existing MSCOCO human annotations for annotated settings.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The consistency between POPE Yes/No responses and captions generated by LVLMs was measured. Out of 1303 and 1445 objects given 'No' responses by InstructBLIP and MiniGPT-4 respectively, merely 0 and 5 of those objects were referenced in captions. Out of 664 and 1034 objects mentioned in captions, 664 and 961 respectively received a 'Yes' verdict, confirming robust correlation between caption content and POPE responses. Performance gap between annotation-based and SEEM-based POPE was also noted (e.g., F1 Score 71.37 vs. 62.70 for MiniGPT-4 under Adversarial setting), attributed to finer granularity of SEEM segmentation results.
rai:annotationsPerItem: 6 polling questions per image (l=6), with a 1:1 ratio of ground-truth to non-existent objects (3 'Yes' and 3 'No' questions per image).
rai:machineAnnotationTools: SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) by Zou et al. (2023) for automatic image segmentation and object annotation on unannotated datasets. ChatGPT for VQA evaluation assistance.
rai:dataSocialImpact: Object hallucination in LVLMs hinders their safe use in real-world deployment, as hallucinated objects may result in unexpected consequences. For example, an autonomous driving system with incorrect understanding of the external environment could make wrong decisions when encountering unexpected events, potentially leading to serious safety issues. The work also highlights risks for blind users relying on computer-generated captions of images.
rai:dataBiases: Visual instruction datasets of LVLMs are mostly constructed based on MSCOCO and share a similar unbalanced object distribution where top frequent objects occupy a major part of the dataset. LVLMs are prone to hallucinate frequently appearing objects and frequently co-occurring objects in the visual instruction data. Approximately half of hallucinated objects in each image belong to the top 10 frequently appearing COCO objects, and more than half are among the top 10 frequently co-occurring objects. LVLMs using synthetic visual instructions generated by unimodal LLMs may involve unexpected descriptive information inconsistent with images.
rai:dataLimitations: The evaluation focuses only on object hallucination and does not consider other aspects of LVLM capacity, so higher scores do not necessarily indicate stronger overall capacity. Evaluation is conducted on a subset of the validation set due to computation resource limitations, and results may be affected by data distribution. POPE uses a matching-based method to determine Yes/No answers, but LVLMs may occasionally fail to provide explicit Yes/No answers, leading to inaccurate evaluation. When combined with automatic segmentation tools, annotated objects may be inconsistent with human annotations, causing divergence in evaluation results. Only a small number of LVLMs are compared, excluding some recently released or closed-source ones.
rai:dataUseCases: Testing and evaluation of object hallucination in large vision-language models. The dataset supports evaluation of LVLMs on binary object presence classification tasks, analysis of hallucination patterns related to object frequency and co-occurrence, and benchmarking of LVLMs across different difficulty levels (Random, Popular, Adversarial settings). Can be extended to unannotated datasets using automatic segmentation tools.
